items.stem: What is the main difference between descriptive and narrative writing?
options: Description focuses on evoking a place, moment or person; narrative develops a sequence of events
Description is always in the present tense
items.answer: Description focuses on evoking a place, moment or person; narrative develops a sequence of events
items.markingKey: Descriptive pieces should not turn into stories with plot.

items.stem: This sentence appears in the opening of a short story: ‘Nobody noticed the hairline crack spreading slowly across the dam wall.’ Identify the technique and explain how it engages the reader.
items.answer: Foreshadowing: the detail hints at disaster and creates dramatic irony.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark, 1 for each of the following up to the maximum: identifies foreshadowing; explains the effect (the detail hints at disaster and creates dramatic irony); comments on its suitability for the opening of a short story.

items.stem: This sentence appears in the opening of a short story: ‘I never lie, of course. Well, hardly ever. And never about anything important.’ Identify the technique and explain how it engages the reader.
items.answer: Unreliable narrator: the self-contradiction makes the reader distrust the narrator.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark, 1 for each of the following up to the maximum: identifies unreliable narrator; explains the effect (the self-contradiction makes the reader distrust the narrator); comments on its suitability for the opening of a short story.

items.stem: How does discursive writing differ from argumentative writing?
options: Discursive writing explores several viewpoints in a balanced way; argumentative writing persuades towards one view
items.answer: Discursive writing explores several viewpoints in a balanced way; argumentative writing persuades towards one view

items.stem: Sipho uses this sentence in an argumentative speech: ‘It is not a cost; it is an investment.’ Explain how it persuades the audience.
items.answer: Antithesis: the contrast reframes the issue.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark, 1 for each of the following up to the maximum: identifies the technique; explains how it persuades; comments on its likely effect on the audience.

items.stem: Lina uses this sentence in an argumentative speech: ‘Critics say the scheme is too expensive. Yet the cost of doing nothing is far greater.’ Explain how it persuades the audience.
items.answer: Concession and rebuttal: the objection is acknowledged and then overturned.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks, 1 for each of the following up to the maximum: identifies the technique; explains how it persuades; comments on its likely effect on the audience.

items.stem: You are writing an argumentative essay in which you agree with the statement ‘Fast fashion should be taxed heavily.’ Write a paragraph (about 80 words) that raises a likely counter-argument and rebuts it.
items.answer: A paragraph that fairly states a counter-argument, then rebuts it with evidence or reasoning, using a contrastive connective.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks, 1 per valid point: counter-argument stated fairly; rebuttal with reasoning or evidence; contrastive connective; persuasive language; accuracy.

items.stem: ‘Libraries are more important than ever.’ Write a letter to a national newspaper arguing your point of view. (600–900 words)
items.answer: Indicative content: a clear, sustained stance; logically sequenced, developed arguments; evidence and examples; rhetorical devices (ethos, pathos, logos, antithesis, tricolon); counter-arguments rebutted; a forceful conclusion; register suited to the form; accuracy.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10 (AO2 writing: content, structure, style and accuracy). Level 5 (9–10): highly effective, sophisticated writing for the purpose and audience; ambitious, precise vocabulary and a wide range of controlled structures; cohesive, deliberately shaped organisation; consistently accurate; Level 4 (7–8): effective writing with a clear sense of purpose and audience; a good range of vocabulary and structures; well organised; mostly accurate; Level 3 (5–6): generally clear writing appropriate to the task; some range of vocabulary and structures; organisation mostly secure; some errors; Level 2 (3–4): some sense of purpose; limited vocabulary and sentence variety; organisation uneven; errors sometimes affect meaning; Level 1 (1–2): little sense of purpose or audience; simple, repetitive expression; frequent errors. Indicative content: a clear, sustained stance; logically sequenced, developed arguments; evidence and examples; rhetorical devices (ethos, pathos, logos, antithesis, tricolon); counter-arguments rebutted; a forceful conclusion; register suited to the form; accuracy.

items.stem: A student’s plan for ‘Write a discursive essay on whether competitive sport should be compulsory in schools.’ is: ‘Intro – stuff about phones. Middle – more stuff. End – conclusion.’ Explain why this plan is weak and how it could be improved.
items.answer: Too vague: no specific ideas, evidence or progression.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark, 1 for each of the following up to the maximum: identifies the weakness; explains its consequence for the final piece; a specific improvement.

items.stem: In timed conditions you have five minutes to plan a response to ‘Write a discursive essay exploring whether space exploration is worth the cost.’ Write a concise plan.
items.answer: A plan with: introduction framing the debate; viewpoint 1: scientific discovery and inspiration; viewpoint 2: urgent problems on Earth that need funding; evaluation; reasoned conclusion.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks, 1 per valid point: introduction framing the debate; viewpoint 1: scientific discovery and inspiration; viewpoint 2: urgent problems on Earth that need funding; evaluation; reasoned conclusion.

items.stem: In timed conditions you have five minutes to plan a response to ‘Write a story about two strangers stranded together.’ Write a concise plan.
items.answer: A plan with: an opening hook or technique; development/complication; climax or turning point; ending (e.g. cyclical or reflective); notes on atmosphere and techniques.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks, 1 per valid point: an opening hook or technique; development/complication; climax or turning point; ending (e.g. cyclical or reflective); notes on atmosphere and techniques.
